title: Baby not breathing at birth
desc: This station involves leading the first steps of resuscitation of a term baby who is floppy and apnoeic at birth and then, once the neonatal team has taken over, taking a focused history from the midwife, then interpreting the resuscitation record against the ANZCOR SpO2 targets, the cord gas and the blood glucose, outlining post-resuscitation care with doses for this baby, and safety-netting the family.
stem: You are the junior doctor called to the birth suite of a metropolitan maternity hospital. A term baby (39+2 weeks, 3.4 kg) has just been born by vaginal birth. The baby is floppy and is not breathing. A midwife is assisting you at the resuscitaire. The mother is awake and anxious.
tasks: Lead the initial assessment and resuscitation of the baby, telling the examiner what you assess and do, including the SpO2 target you are using. Once the neonatal team has arrived and taken over the ventilation, take a focused history from the midwife (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you the resuscitation record, the cord blood gas and a blood glucose level. Interpret them, then outline your management approach, with doses for this baby, and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: you are the midwife at the birth. The mother is in the bed nearby (the examiner or a second student voices her). Do what the candidate asks, and answer only what is asked. The neonatal registrar arrives 3 minutes after the candidate calls (if the candidate has not called by 3 minutes, the midwife presses the emergency bell and the registrar arrives 2 minutes later). The registrar takes over the ventilation, and the examiner says: "The registrar has the airway now. Please take a focused history from the midwife."

Opening line: "The baby's out. Floppy and not breathing."

Examination findings: the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings as the candidate says what they assess. When the candidate starts mask ventilation, say there is no chest rise until they say they will reposition the head to neutral, check the mask seal and give jaw support; then say the chest is rising. The baby's heart rate and SpO2 after that are given in Part 2 as the resuscitation record, so if the candidate asks, say: "Tell me what you would do with each heart rate and SpO2 you might see." The candidate should state their plan (for example, what they would do if the heart rate stayed below 60, or the SpO2 stayed below target).

History (give only when asked):

  • Term, 39+2 weeks by an early dating scan. Single baby.
  • Liquor clear, no meconium. Membranes ruptured 4 hours before the birth.
  • The CTG was normal until the second stage. Then the fetal heart rate dropped to about 70 for the last 8 minutes before the birth. Second stage lasted about 50 minutes; normal vaginal birth, no instruments.
  • No pethidine, morphine or general anaesthetic in labour; nitrous oxide only. No maternal fever.
  • Pregnancy: GBS negative, normal glucose tolerance test (no diabetes), normal morphology scan with no anomalies, no maternal medicines apart from pregnancy vitamins.
  • This is the mother's first baby. She is well.

Mother: she is frightened and keeps asking, "Is my baby alive? Why isn't my baby crying?" She wants to hold the baby.

Questions to ask if the candidate speaks with her: "Why didn't my baby breathe?" "Will my baby have brain damage?" "Can I hold my baby?"
guide:
In Part 1, the candidate leads the first minutes. The examiner gives the findings at birth from the Exam findings and confirms chest rise once the candidate corrects the airway. The heart rate and SpO2 responses come in Part 2, so in Part 1 credit a clear stated plan (compressions only if HR stays below 60/min after 30 seconds of effective ventilation; more oxygen only if SpO2 is below target despite effective ventilation). The gestation and liquor questions belong at the start; the fuller labour and pregnancy history comes once the registrar has taken over the ventilation. Management items for the resuscitation can be earned in either part. In Part 2, hand over the results and ask the questions in order.

A high-performing candidate takes charge, calls for help, warms the baby, starts ventilation in air within the first minute and confirms chest rise, asks the key history questions, and states the minute-specific ANZCOR SpO2 targets. In Part 2 they read the heart rate and SpO2 record correctly, interpret the cord gas against the cooling threshold, treat the hypoglycaemia with correct doses, plan special care nursery admission with neurological observation, give honest, empathic communication and a structured handover, and give specific return advice.

A borderline candidate warms and ventilates but does not troubleshoot chest rise, plans compressions over ineffective ventilation, ignores the SpO2 targets, misses the hypoglycaemia, and gives vague communication or generic advice such as "come back if worried".
explain:
Initial steps and ventilation

Most newborns who are not breathing respond to warmth, a clear airway and effective ventilation. The heart rate is the most sensitive indicator of response. Start in air (21% oxygen) for babies of 35 weeks or more and confirm chest rise; if there is none, correct the airway and the mask seal before anything else.

Targeted oxygen

Use preductal (right wrist or hand) SpO2. The ANZCOR Guideline 13.4 targets are: 1 min 60 to 70%, 2 min 65 to 85%, 3 min 70 to 90%, 4 min 75 to 90%, 5 min 80 to 90%, 10 min 85 to 90%; the upper limit is capped at 90% to avoid giving too much oxygen. Increase oxygen if below target despite effective ventilation, as was done at 3 minutes here, and avoid exceeding the upper limit.

Compressions

Hypoxic bradycardia usually reverses with lung inflation, as it did here. Start compressions only if HR is below 60/min after 30 seconds of effective ventilation: 3:1 with 100% oxygen. Compressions over ineffective ventilation do not help. Adrenaline (10 to 30 micrograms/kg IV via a UVC, repeated every 3 to 5 minutes, ANZCOR Guideline 13.7) is for a heart rate that stays below 60/min despite both.

Post-resuscitation care

Check temperature (36.5 to 37.5 °C), BGL and cord gas. A BGL below 2.6 mmol/L is always treated (Safer Care Victoria): send a laboratory glucose to confirm without delaying treatment, give 40% glucose gel 0.5 mL/kg (1.7 mL) followed by a feed and recheck the BGL 30 to 60 minutes later, moving to IV 10% glucose (2 mL/kg = 6.8 mL, then an infusion) if it stays low despite gel and feeds or the baby is unwell. Therapeutic hypothermia is considered for a baby of 35 weeks or more with moderate to severe encephalopathy and evidence of hypoxia-ischaemia (for example pH 7.0 or below, or a base deficit of 12 mmol/L or more, in the first hour), and works best started within 6 hours of birth; this baby's gas does not meet the threshold, but neurological observation continues. Admit to special care or NICU and discuss with the parents honestly.

Safety netting

In the nursery, poor tone, poor feeding, altered alertness, seizures, apnoea or hypoglycaemia need urgent review. At discharge, parents should call 000 for colour change, breathing pauses or seizures and return for poor feeding, floppiness, breathing difficulty, temperature problems, jaundice or fewer wet nappies, with paediatric follow-up arranged.
points: Most apnoeic newborns respond to warmth, airway positioning and effective ventilation; HR rise is the key sign of effective ventilation.
Preductal SpO2 targets (ANZCOR Guideline 13.4): 1 min 60-70%, 2 min 65-85%, 3 min 70-90%, 4 min 75-90%, 5 min 80-90%, 10 min 85-90%.
Start in air at 35 weeks or more; increase oxygen only if SpO2 is below the target despite effective ventilation.
Correct ventilation first; start 3:1 compressions with 100% oxygen only if HR is below 60/min after 30 s of effective ventilation.
After resuscitation check temperature (36.5-37.5 °C), BGL (treat below 2.6 mmol/L) and cord gas; babies needing PPV are admitted for monitoring, with clear discharge criteria and return advice.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene and puts on gloves, introduces self, takes the team-leader role and gives the midwife clear tasks.
Speaks calmly to the mother during the resuscitation, telling her what is happening.
History
Asks the midwife the key questions at the start: gestation and whether the liquor is clear or meconium-stained.
Once the neonatal team has taken over, takes a focused labour history:

kids.x: The fetal bradycardia: when it started and how long it lasted
Rupture of membranes and maternal fever
Pethidine, morphine or a general anaesthetic in the hours before birth

check.x: Takes a focused pregnancy history: diabetes, GBS status, anomalies on scans and maternal medicines.
Examination

Notes the time of birth and assesses tone, breathing and heart rate (by stethoscope) within seconds: recognises a floppy, apnoeic baby with HR 70 (below 100) and starts resuscitation without waiting for an Apgar score.
Within the first minute dries the baby, removes wet linen, wraps, puts on a hat, positions the head neutral and gives brief stimulation only.
Opens the airway: neutral position and jaw support, looks in the mouth and suctions only if obstructed.
Applies the SpO2 probe to the right wrist or hand (preductal) and states the ANZCOR targets: 1 min 60 to 70%, 2 min 65 to 85%, 3 min 70 to 90%, 4 min 75 to 90%, 5 min 80 to 90%, 10 min 85 to 90%.
Measures the temperature (36.2 °C) and keeps the baby warm.
Once the baby is stable, does a brief newborn check: palate, spine, abdomen, limbs and any dysmorphic features or birth injury.
Interpretation
Interprets the heart rate: the rise from 70 to 120 at 2 minutes and 140 at 3 minutes shows the ventilation is effective, so compressions are not needed.

Interprets the SpO2 against the targets: 62% at 1 minute and 66% at 2 minutes are in range; 68% at 3 minutes is below 70% despite effective ventilation, so increasing the oxygen was right; 85% at 5 minutes is in range (80 to 90%).
States the temperature of 36.6 °C at 5 minutes is normal (36.5 to 37.5 °C) and that both cooling and overheating should be avoided.

Interprets the cord gas (pH 7.18, base excess -8) as a mild acidosis that does not meet the gas criteria for therapeutic hypothermia (pH 7.0 or below, or a base deficit of 12 mmol/L or more), with ongoing neurological observation.
Interprets the BGL of 2.2 mmol/L as hypoglycaemia (below 2.6 mmol/L), which is common after resuscitation.

Gives the likely cause: perinatal hypoxia from the acute fetal bradycardia, and considers other causes (maternal opioids, infection, airway obstruction, a congenital or neuromuscular problem), with reasons they are less likely here.
Management
Calls the neonatal team early, as soon as the baby needs ventilation.
Starts positive pressure ventilation within the first minute at 40 to 60 breaths/min in air (21% oxygen), as for any baby of 35 weeks or more, and confirms chest rise and a rising heart rate.

Troubleshoots absent chest rise: repositions the head, gives jaw support and improves the mask seal, opens the mouth, suctions if obstructed, then increases inflation pressure. Ventilation is corrected before any compressions.
Increases the oxygen when SpO2 is below the target for that minute despite effective ventilation, and titrates so that SpO2 does not go above the upper target (90%), weaning towards air.
States the plan if the heart rate does not respond:

kids.x: Chest compressions only if HR stays below 60/min after 30 seconds of effective ventilation: 3 compressions to 1 breath with 100% oxygen, stopping when HR is 60/min or more

IV adrenaline via a UVC if HR stays below 60/min despite effective ventilation and compressions: 10 to 30 micrograms/kg = 34 to 102 micrograms for 3.4 kg (0.1 to 0.3 mL/kg of 1:10 000 = 0.34 to 1.02 mL), repeated every 3 to 5 minutes

check.x: Treats the hypoglycaemia: 40% glucose gel 0.5 mL/kg = 1.7 mL for 3.4 kg into the cheek, then a breastfeed or expressed colostrum, and repeats the BGL 30 to 60 minutes later; escalates to IV 10% glucose (2 mL/kg = 6.8 mL, then an infusion) as the hypoglycaemia guideline sets out if the BGL stays below 2.6 mmol/L despite gel and feeds, or the baby is unwell.
Admits to the special care nursery (or NICU), not routine postnatal care, with monitoring of HR, RR, SpO2, temperature, BGL and neurological observations for encephalopathy over the first hours.

Explains to the mother in plain language that the baby needed help to breathe, probably because of low oxygen before birth when the heart rate dropped, and is now breathing and crying; answers the question about brain injury honestly (the quick recovery and the gas are reassuring, and the baby will be watched closely); arranges skin-to-skin contact once stable.
Gives a structured handover (ISBAR) to the neonatal team: gestation, weight, time of birth, interventions and their times, response, cord gas and BGL.
Safety netting

States the signs that need urgent neonatal review in the nursery: poor tone, poor suck or feeding, reduced alertness or irritability, seizures, apnoea, or a low BGL, as encephalopathy needs assessment for cooling within 6 hours of birth.

Gives return advice after discharge: call 000 for blue or grey colour, pauses in breathing or seizures, and return to the ED for poor feeding, floppiness or sleepiness, fast or laboured breathing, a temperature below 36.5 °C or a fever, jaundice, or fewer wet nappies.
States discharge criteria (feeding well, temperature 36.5 to 37.5 °C, BGL 2.6 mmol/L or more, stable observations) and arranges paediatric follow-up.

ask: Talk me through the resuscitation record. How did the baby respond, and how do the SpO2 readings compare with the targets?
What do the cord gas and the blood glucose show, and why do you think this baby did not breathe at birth?
What is your management now? Include where the baby will be cared for and doses for this baby.
What will you tell the mother, and what will you hand over to the neonatal team?
What would worry you over the next hours, and what advice will the parents get at discharge?
